tools: scikit-learn splitters for k-fold cross-validation; the stratified one keeps the class mix the same in every fold.
Independent rows (KFold with shuffle=True); any classification task (StratifiedKFold, the default for classifiers when cv=5).
RepeatedStratifiedKFold for small data; a single holdout for huge data
Splitters that keep every row of a group (patient, user, store) in the same fold.
Several rows per entity and the model will meet new entities; pass groups=.
LeaveOneGroupOut (one fold per hospital or site)
Expanding-window splits: train on the past, test on the block after it, with an optional gap.
Forecasting and any data where order matters.
Run cross-validation for one (cross_val_score) or several metrics (cross_validate, with train scores and timings).
Every model comparison; wrap preprocessing in a Pipeline so it refits per fold.
Regression evaluation; as CV scorers use neg_root_mean_squared_error, neg_mean_absolute_error, r2.
Scoring quantile forecasts when over- and under-prediction cost different amounts.
Counts of TN, FP, FN, TP (negative class first) and per-class precision, recall and F1.
First look at any classifier, at the threshold you'll use.
Wrappers (since scikit-learn 1.5) that tune the decision threshold by CV for any scorer or cost, or fix it.
Whenever 0.5 isn't the right cut: imbalance, asymmetric costs.
Picking the threshold by hand on validation predictions
Threshold-free summaries: ROC AUC (ranking probability) and average precision (PR curve summary).
Comparing rankers; AP when positives are rare.
Library of resamplers (SMOTE, RandomOverSampler, RandomUnderSampler…) and a Pipeline that resamples only during fit.
Weak learners on rare classes; huge majority classes to undersample.
Fits Platt (sigmoid), isotonic or temperature calibration with cross-fitting; wrap a fitted model in FrozenEstimator to calibrate on held-out data.
When predicted probabilities are used as probabilities (prices, risks, expected cost).
Bucketed predicted probability vs observed frequency: the reliability diagram.
Exhaustive search over a grid, or random draws from distributions (e.g. scipy.stats.loguniform), each scored by CV.
Small grids for 1–2 knobs; random search for 3+ knobs.
Successive halving: many candidates on a small budget, the best third gets three times more; experimental, enable with from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv.
When a cheap early score (few rows) predicts the final one.
Define-by-run hyperparameter optimisation: create_study, trial.suggest_float/int/categorical, TPE by default (multivariate since 5.0), pruning with trial.report / should_prune.
Expensive models with many knobs; conditional search spaces.
Training and validation scores vs training size, or vs one hyperparameter; plot with LearningCurveDisplay / ValidationCurveDisplay.
Deciding between more data, more capacity and more regularisation.
acronyms: Rotating train/test splits so every row is tested once, then averaging the scores.
Average size of the misses; minimised by predicting the median.
Average squared miss (and its square root, in the target's units); minimised by the mean, punishes big misses.
1 − your squared error ÷ the mean-guesser's; 0 = no better than the mean, negative = worse.
Average of |error| ÷ |actual|; explodes near zero actuals and rewards forecasting low.
Divides each miss by the average of |forecast| and |actual|, capping each term at 200%.
MAE divided by the MAE of a naive “same as last period” forecast; safe across series of any scale.
RMSE on log(1 + y): judges relative error for targets spanning orders of magnitude.
True positive / false positive / false negative / true negative
The four cells of a confusion matrix: catches, false alarms, misses and correct rejections.
TPR = recall = TP ÷ positives; FPR = FP ÷ negatives = 1 − specificity. The axes of the ROC curve.
Correlation between predicted and true labels using all four confusion cells; near 0 for useless models.
Curve of TPR vs FPR over all thresholds; named after WWII radar receiver operators.
Probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative; 0.5 random, 1 perfect.
Precision vs recall over all thresholds; AP averages precision at each recall step. Honest under imbalance.
Creates minority points on segments between a minority point and one of its k nearest minority neighbours.
Average gap between bucket predictions and observed frequencies, weighted by bucket size.
Bayesian-style search that models where good and bad trials live and samples where good ÷ bad is highest; Optuna's default.
terms: Split into k folds, train on k − 1, test on the last, rotate, report mean ± spread. k = 5 or 10 is standard.
Keeping the class proportions the same in every fold or split.
Rows of the same entity on both sides of a split, so the model recognises the entity instead of learning the task.
An inner CV loop tunes hyperparameters; an outer loop scores the whole tune-then-train procedure.
The best of many noisy scores is optimistic; the more you compare, the bigger the inflation.
Charges τ per unit of under-prediction and 1 − τ per unit of over-prediction; minimised by the τ-quantile.
Table of predicted vs actual classes: TP, FP, FN, TN.
Share of flagged cases that are really positive: TP ÷ (TP + FP).
Share of real positives that were caught: TP ÷ (TP + FN).
Share of real negatives correctly let through: TN ÷ (TN + FP).
Harmonic mean of precision and recall; F-beta weights recall β times as much.
A useless model can be highly accurate when one class dominates (“always legit” = 99.83% on card fraud).
Flag when p > C<sub>FP</sub> ÷ (C<sub>FP</sub> + C<sub>FN</sub>) for calibrated probabilities, or pick the cheapest threshold on validation data.
Average of −log(probability given to what happened); punishes confident mistakes hardest.
The share of positives in the data; precision and PR curves depend on it, ROC does not.
Make each minority example count more in the loss, e.g. n ÷ (2 × n<sub>class</sub>) for “balanced”.
Duplicate minority rows or drop majority rows to balance the training set; only inside training folds.
Keep the model, change the cut-off on its scores to trade precision for recall.
Imbalanced data (often the best first fix)
Predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: among predictions of 70%, about 70% happen.
Plot of bucketed predicted probability vs observed frequency; the diagonal is perfect calibration.
Mean squared error of predicted probabilities; lower is better. Proposed for weather forecasts in 1950.
Calibration by a 2-parameter logistic fit on the model's scores.
Calibration by the best non-decreasing step function; flexible but needs ~1,000+ rows.
Divide logits by one fitted number T before the softmax; the standard fix for overconfident neural nets.
Try every combination of a few values per knob.
Draw each knob at random from a range; covers important knobs far more densely than a grid for the same budget.
Use the trials so far to model the score and choose the next trial where improvement is likely.
Start many settings on a small budget, keep the best fraction, give them more, repeat; Hyperband runs several such brackets.
Stop a trial whose intermediate score is worse than earlier trials at the same step.
Expected test error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise.
Training and validation error vs number of training rows: tells you whether more data will help.
Training and validation error vs one hyperparameter: shows the complexity sweet spot.
Underfitting (both errors high and close) vs overfitting (training error much lower than validation).
